title: Affine geometry and matrix groups
statement:
Use the coefficient convention of [sk-d-linear]: $k$ is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and $V$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space. An affine variety over $k$ is $\operatorname{Spec}B$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] for a finitely generated commutative $k$-algebra $B$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra, def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient] that is reduced, meaning that it has no nonzero nilpotents. Closed subvarieties are $\operatorname{Spec}(B/J)$ for radical ideals $J$ (an ideal is radical if $b^r\in J$, $r\geq1$, implies $b\in J$); the inclusion is induced by $B\to B/J$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Regular maps $\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}B$ are the maps induced by $k$-algebra homomorphisms $B\to C$, in the opposite direction. The Zariski closed sets are $V(J)=\{\mathfrak p:J\subseteq\mathfrak p\}$; in a polynomial presentation of $B$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] these are polynomial zero loci.

The closure of a subset is the intersection of all closed sets containing it. As in this sketch, connected means having no decomposition into two nonempty disjoint open sets, and irreducible means not being a union of two proper closed sets. These two no-decomposition conditions allow the empty space; no nonemptiness condition is implicit in these words here. A constructible set, in the underlying space of an affine variety, is a finite union of locally closed sets, that is, intersections of an open and a closed set [def-weil-locally-closed-subset]. Dimension is the Krull dimension of the coordinate algebra [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], the supremum of the lengths of strict chains of prime ideals (with value $-\infty$ for the zero algebra).

Choose a basis of $V$, put $n=\dim_kV$, $P=k[x_{ij}:1\leq i,j\leq n]$, $D=\det(x_{ij})$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], and $A=P[1/D]$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. The general linear group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is identified in this basis with $\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}=\operatorname{Spec}A$. For $n\geq1$ this is the general linear group scheme of [def-sc-general-linear-group]; for $n=0$ the empty determinant is $1$, $A=k$, and $\mathrm{GL}_{0,k}=\operatorname{Spec}k$ with its trivial group law. A group scheme and its homomorphisms mean [def-sc-group-scheme]. The $R$-points of $\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}$, for any commutative $k$-algebra $R$, are the invertible $n\times n$ matrices over $R$. Write $\Delta=m^*:A\to A\otimes_kA$, $\varepsilon=e^*:A\to k$ and $S=i^*:A\to A$ for the coordinate maps of multiplication, identity and inversion. Thus $\Delta(x_{ij})=\sum_r x_{ir}\otimes x_{rj}$, $\varepsilon(x_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$, and $S((x_{ij}))=(x_{ij})^{-1}$, with the values on $D^{-1}$ forced by these formulas. Tensor products here are the commutative algebra tensor products of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property].

A matrix algebraic group is a closed subgroup scheme $G\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] cut out by a Hopf ideal $I$ of $A$, not required to be radical. Explicitly, for the quotient map $q:A\to A/I$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient], the Hopf-ideal conditions are $\varepsilon(I)=0$, $(q\otimes q)\Delta(I)=0$ in $(A/I)\otimes_k(A/I)$, and $S(I)\subseteq I$. The scheme is $G=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$, included in $\operatorname{Spec}A$ by $\operatorname{Spec}q$, and its group operations are induced by these three coordinate maps. Its $R$-points are exactly the invertible matrices over $R$ on which all equations in $I$ vanish. Multiplication and inversion are regular, and a homomorphism means a homomorphism of group schemes over $k$, equivalently a regular group homomorphism. A homomorphism $G\to\mathrm{GL}_{m,k}$ is a rational representation of $G$ on $k^m$. When writing products we identify $G(k)$ with its matrices.

The identity component $G^\circ$ is the reduced closed subgroup on the connected component $C$ of the identity point in the underlying space of $G$. Concretely $C$ is the union of the connected subsets containing that point, and its reduced closed structure is given by the ideal $\bigcap_{\mathfrak p\in C}\mathfrak p$ in $A/I$, or by its inverse image in $A$; reduction means [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction]. The center $Z(G)$ is the reduced closed subgroup of $G$ whose $k$-points commute with every $h\in G(k)$, rather than the centralizer in the ambient $\mathrm{GL}(V)$. Concretely, if $X=(x_{ij})$ over $A$, its ideal in $A$ is the radical $\sqrt{J}$ of the sum $J=I+(\text{all entries of }Xh-hX:\ h\in G(k))$, the ideal generated by $I$ and these entries; it contains $I$, so $Z(G)=\operatorname{Spec}(A/\sqrt J)$ is a closed subscheme of $G$, and its $k$-points are the $g\in G(k)$ with $gh=hg$ for all $h\in G(k)$.
